1.title: Executing, Status Reporting and Closure
1.text: Welcome to Module 9. This module follows the project through the rest of its life: doing the work, telling the truth about progress, and ending properly. In Part 1, we look at executing: directing and managing the work, implementing approved changes, and executing in agile and hybrid projects. Part 2 covers metrics and status. Part 3 covers closure, including acceptance, transition and benefits.

1.title: Where This Module Sits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits. In the Process domain, this module covers three tasks. Task one, the integrated plan and delivery, shows up here as execution. Task nine: evaluate project status, with metrics, analysis and reporting. Task ten: manage project closure. Execution questions test discipline: follow the plan, change it only through the process, keep the records current and protect value. Status questions test honest, audience-fit reporting. Closure questions test acceptance, readiness and formal completion.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do six things. Direct and manage the work, and implement approved changes correctly. Execute in agile and hybrid projects on real capacity. Build metrics, avoid measurement pitfalls and report status to each audience. Manage artifacts so they are current and findable. Set closure criteria, obtain acceptance and check transition readiness. And conclude financial, contractual and administrative work, and hand over benefits.

1.title: Case Check-In: Executing the Microgrid
1.text: Now we execute the microgrid. In the build lane, work is authorized per the plan, and handoffs and reporting lines with Harlow Construction are defined. In the software lane, iterations come from the backlog on actual capacity, with daily coordination and reviews with real users. Baseline changes go to the change board, and backlog changes go to the product owner. Throughout, collect work performance data every iteration, remove impediments, capture lessons as you go, and engage the lab and the neighbors as planned.

1.title: Executing: Key Terms
1.text: Key terms. The Executing Focus Area covers the actions performed to complete the work consistently with the currently agreed course of action. Manage Project Execution leads and performs the work and implements approved changes. Work performance data is raw observations: actual dates, costs, defects and story points. A change request is a formal proposal to modify a document, deliverable or baseline, and types include corrective action, preventive action and defect repair. The change log lists submitted changes and their disposition. The issue log records issues. And the project management information system supports all of it.

1.title: What Runs in Executing
1.text: Eight processes run in the Executing Focus Area. Three in Governance: Manage Project Execution, Manage Quality Assurance and Manage Project Knowledge. Two in Stakeholders: Manage Stakeholder Engagement and Manage Communications. Two in Resources: Acquire Resources and Lead the Team. And Implement Risk Responses in Risk. Scope, schedule and finance have no executing-only process. Their work is planned in Planning. And it is controlled in Monitoring and Controlling, which runs in parallel and receives the work performance data.

1.title: Manage Project Execution
1.text: Manage Project Execution aims to align the knowledge and skills of the team toward the objectives. It produces deliverables from activities carried out according to the plan. And it makes technical and functional work fit together. Inputs include plan components, logs, the schedule, the risk register and approved change requests. Tools are expert judgment, the information system and meetings. Outputs are deliverables, work performance data, an issue log, change requests and updates. It also reviews the impact of all changes. And it implements the approved ones. Quality has two routes: process assurance, and deliverable quality through scope control.

1.title: Directing and Managing Day to Day
1.text: A good execution day has five habits. Coordinate: a short daily meeting on what was done, what is planned and what blocks progress. Perform: work per the plan and the definition of done. Record work performance data consistently, so monitoring can turn it into information. Unblock: evaluate, prioritize and remove impediments, and check that a resolved blocker has really ended, not just moved. Communicate: engage stakeholders and make progress visible. Start well with a kickoff aligned on vision, plan, roles and team agreements.

1.title: Keep the Plan Alive
1.text: Keep the plan alive. When reality or value changes, use the change process in predictive work, or reprioritize the backlog in adaptive work. The plan is not an unchangeable contract. Keep information in the project management information system and in a controlled repository, with configuration control, so people use current versions. Assign and coordinate work with defined handoffs and reporting lines, including for vendors. Capture lessons during the work, not only at the end. And protect value: watch the business case and external changes, and do not let output replace outcomes.

1.title: Implementing Approved Changes
1.text: Here is the change loop. Any stakeholder may request a change. Requests are assessed through integrated change control, with impact on all domains. The change is approved, deferred or rejected, and the disposition goes in the change log and is communicated, including to those whose requests were deferred or rejected. Execution then implements approved changes: corrective actions, preventive actions and defect repairs. And update everything affected, such as designs, schedule, baselines, backlog, requirements and the risk register. Approval is not complete until the work and the documents reflect it.

1.title: Unapproved Changes
1.text: Do not make unapproved changes, even harmless-looking or free ones. A free design improvement, or a higher-capacity part from a vendor, still needs impact assessment on power, piping, safety and testing. Checking that tests pass does not replace configuration review. If you find an unapproved change, do not just remove it or keep it unreviewed: evaluate the impact and submit it through change control. Deferred or rejected requests are communicated to the requester. And gold plating is unapproved scope, a form of scope growth.

1.title: Executing in Adaptive and Hybrid Work
1.text: In adaptive work, iterations are small execution cycles. Plan from the backlog on actual capacity. Work within the definition of done and hold the daily coordination meeting. Review the increment with stakeholders, with real feedback time. Hold a retrospective that commits to a few improvements. Protect the iteration: mid-iteration requests go to the product owner and the backlog. The project manager represents the team's capacity. Make progress visible with boards and burn charts. In hybrid work, fixed regulatory or contractual commitments run under change control, while the iterative layer adapts inside them.

1.title: Iteration Execution
1.text: An iteration is a small execution cycle. Plan it from the backlog on actual capacity. Work to the definition of done, with automated tests and compliance checks built in. Review the increment with feedback time and real users. Retrospect, and commit to a few improvements. If an executive asks for an urgent feature mid-iteration, send the request to the product owner. Show the trade-off and the capacity. Protect the committed scope unless the team and product owner agree a swap.

1.title: Event Routing: What Goes Where
1.text: Where does an event go? A new request or idea goes to change control in predictive work, or to the product owner's backlog in adaptive work. A risk that occurs is now an issue: run the planned response and log it. A blocker is removed. A recurring blocker needs action, not another log entry. A free or harmless extra is not implemented unreviewed: assess its impact and use change control. A missed handoff is fixed by defining the handoff, roles and confirmation points, not by adding meetings. Never skip the record: the logs and the backlog keep decisions alive through turnover and audits.

1.title: Executing in Predictive, Agile and Hybrid Work
1.text: Execution differs by approach. Predictive: work packages and activities against baselines, authorized per the plan. Coordination is through status meetings and dependency management. Change uses formal requests and a change board, and data comes from actuals against baseline and earned value. Agile: iterations from a prioritized backlog, and the team pulls work from the sprint backlog. Coordination is through daily meetings and shared boards. Change is backlog reprioritization, and data comes from velocity, burn charts and accepted work. Hybrid: change control for the baselined envelope only.

1.title: Execution Traps: What PMI Expects
1.text: The traps for execution. Approved changes must be implemented and the documents updated. Unapproved changes, even free ones, go through change control. Mid-iteration requests go to the product owner, and iterations are planned on actual capacity. Remove impediments, and define handoffs, roles and reporting lines rather than adding review meetings. Collect work performance data consistently, and make progress visible where stakeholders can see it. Build quality in, capture lessons while working, and resolve conflict early and at the source.

1.title: Part 1 Recap
1.text: Let us recap Part 1. Execution means performing the work, recording data, removing blockers and communicating. Changes are assessed, approved, implemented, and every affected document updated. Unapproved changes, even free ones, go through change control. In adaptive work, plan on actual capacity, protect the iteration and build quality in. Know where events go: requests, occurred risks, blockers and handoffs. And remember that execution produces deliverables and data, while control analyzes and decides. In Part 2, we turn to status.

2.title: Monitoring and Controlling: Key Terms
2.text: Part 2 covers status. Key terms. Monitoring collects, measures and assesses data, compares actual with planned performance, and reports. Controlling analyzes variances, evaluates alternatives, recommends action and follows up. A leading indicator shows upcoming trends, and a lagging indicator reflects past performance. An input metric measures what goes in, an output metric what is produced, and an outcome metric the value achieved. A dashboard shows progress against key measures, often in red, amber and green. An information radiator is a visible display of status. And reconciliation checks that figures agree across sources and definitions.

2.title: Monitor and Control Project Performance
2.text: The Monitor and Control Project Performance process tracks, reviews and reports overall progress. So stakeholders understand the current state, see actions taken on performance issues, and see forecasts of cost and schedule. It also evaluates whether decisions might enhance the value proposition. It involves evaluating performance against the plan, and tracking resource use, work completed and budget spent. It involves informing stakeholders. And it involves assessing whether deliverables are on track to deliver planned benefits. The diagram splits the work in two. Monitoring collects and assesses data, compares actual with planned, and reports. Controlling analyzes variances, evaluates alternatives, recommends corrective or preventive action, and follows up. If a beneficial decision changes a baseline, use integrated change control.

2.title: Types of Metric
2.text: Metrics come in types. Input metrics measure what goes in: utilization, hours. Output metrics measure what is produced: features, velocity. Outcome metrics measure the value achieved: benefits, usage and satisfaction. Governance prefers outcome metrics. Separately, leading indicators show upcoming trends, such as growing work in progress or disengaged stakeholders, so you can act before a tolerance is crossed. Lagging indicators reflect past performance and are easier to measure, such as variances and deliverables completed. Keep each metric specific, measurable, achievable, realistic and time-bound.

2.title: Developing a Metric Set
2.text: Governance needs three components: target metrics aligned with strategy, signaling mechanisms, usually leading indicators, and feedback mechanisms. To build a metric set, start from the success criteria and the benefits plan. Choose a balanced few: outcome and output, leading and lagging, process and product. Make each metric specific, with a definition, source, owner, frequency, target and threshold. Reconcile the data so sources and definitions agree before reporting. And review and retire metrics that nobody uses or that mislead.

2.title: Typical Metrics by Domain
2.text: Here are typical metrics. Scope: scope definition accuracy, requirements stability and acceptance rate. Schedule: schedule variance and index, milestone variance, velocity, burn charts and cycle time. Finance: cost variance, cost index, estimate at completion, and spend per iteration against value. Quality: defects found and escaped, test coverage and rework. Resources: utilization, downtime, turnover and team satisfaction. Stakeholders: satisfaction, engagement and Net Promoter Score. Risk: open high risks, exposure and reserve use. Benefits: benefits realized, adoption and usage.

2.title: Measurement Pitfalls
2.text: PMBOK 8 names six pitfalls. The Hawthorne effect: measuring changes behavior, so output-only measures push volume over customer value. A vanity metric looks good but informs no decision. Demoralization: unachievable targets sink morale. Misuse: gaming, favoring the short term, or doing easy out-of-sequence work to move an indicator. Confirmation bias: seeing only data that supports your view, so seek disconfirming evidence. And correlation is not causation. Steady velocity can hide falling morale, and a burnup showing scope growth explains slow completion without blaming the team.

2.title: Assess Progress and Analyze Performance
2.text: Techniques for assessing progress. Performance reviews compare actual work with the baseline: dates, percent complete and remaining duration. Variance analysis finds the cause and degree of difference, viewing cost, time, technical and resource variances together. Trend analysis forecasts from history, an early warning of slippage. Earned value integrates scope, cost and schedule. Burn charts, velocity and cycle time show adaptive progress. Root cause analysis finds why before deciding what to do. An SPI above one with a CPI below one means speed was bought.

2.title: From Analysis to Action
2.text: Move from analysis to action. Compare with the thresholds set in the plans. If outside, find the cause, forecast, and evaluate options: corrective or preventive action, reserves, scope or schedule changes. Raise change requests where baselines change, escalate beyond your authority, and report with the decisions needed. Variance within tolerance is monitored. Beyond tolerance, it triggers analysis and action. And forecast total cost with the estimate at completion, not the budget at completion.

2.title: Communicating Project Status
2.text: Know the audience and the decision. The sponsor needs a summary, forecasts, risks and decisions needed. The governance board needs the formats and metrics it requires, for example earned value. The team needs daily boards. Customers need demos and release information. Regulators need formal reports on the required schedule. A new sponsor needs a briefing that reconfirms objectives and support, not just the latest report. Agree formats and frequency in advance, and add exception reports when thresholds are crossed. Support governance: if several bodies ask for different formats, agree one reporting structure.

2.title: Status Report Content and Dashboards
2.text: A status report shows progress since the last report, and forecasts of cost and schedule. It shows scope and change status, and quality and benefit indicators. It lists key risks and issues, decisions or support needed, and the next period. On a dashboard, use red, amber and green with a text explanation for any measure outside its threshold, and drill-down for detail. Here, quality is red because two defects reached the customer: state the cause, the action and the decision needed. Be accurate and timely: share bad news early, with options. Do not let green hide a known problem.

2.title: Case Check-In: Status Reporting for the Microgrid
2.text: On the microgrid, each audience gets a view. The steering committee gets an earned value and milestone view, plus risks and decisions needed. Elena Vasquez gets a one-page summary: forecasts, benefits tracking and escalations. The team gets an iteration board and a burnup chart where everyone can see them. The Eastgate residents get plain-language construction updates on a fixed rhythm. These are different views of one truth. Never let one audience see green while another sees red for the same fact.

2.title: Managing Project Artifacts
2.text: Artifacts are plans, baselines, documents, reports and deliverables. PMBOK 8 lists a sampling, illustrative and not prescriptive, and each organization tailors them. Identify and tailor: pick artifacts that add value for the project's size, risk, regulation and audience. Create and update: give each an owner, a template and a cadence, and review them. Make them accessible: one controlled repository with permissions and version control, so auditors do not hunt through personal drives. Assess effectiveness: are they used, do they inform decisions, what do they cost? And update organizational assets with proven templates.

2.title: Status in Predictive, Agile and Hybrid Work
2.text: Status looks different by approach. Predictive: percent complete, earned value and milestones, with indices and thresholds. Reports and dashboards come monthly or by phase, plus exceptions. Artifacts are formal plans and logs. Agile: accepted working increments, burn charts and velocity. Value delivered, usage and team health matter, shown on radiators and in demos every iteration, with light artifacts. Hybrid: milestones for the envelope and burn charts inside. The pitfalls differ: predictive reporting can describe activity instead of outcomes, and agile reporting can describe output instead of value.

2.title: Status Traps: What PMI Expects
2.text: The traps for status. Report in the form governance needs, and agree formats with each audience. Output is not value: include usage, benefits and outcomes. Prefer leading indicators, and read the schedule and cost indices together. Forecast with the estimate at completion, not the budget at completion. Watch the measurement pitfalls. Keep artifacts current and findable in a controlled repository. Explain red and amber with causes, actions and decisions. Show the real cause of slow progress, such as a burnup with growing scope, instead of pressuring the team.

2.title: Closure: Key Terms
2.text: Now closure. Key terms. The Closing Focus Area formally completes a project, phase or contract, or terminates a project early. Close Project or Phase finalizes all activities, for successful and unsuccessful projects. It archives information and releases resources. And it confirms the extent to which value, or the capability to deliver value, was achieved. Closure criteria are the conditions that must be met before closing, agreed early. Transition readiness is the receiver's ability to run the result. The final report summarizes performance. And the benefits owner tracks benefits after closure.

2.title: When and How a Project Ends
2.text: A project usually ends in one of five ways. The objectives are achieved. A governing body, the sponsor or the team determines the objectives will not or cannot be met. Resources are exhausted. Changes in strategy, priorities or the external environment mean the need no longer exists. Or it is terminated for legal, regulatory or compliance reasons. Early termination for a positive cause means the desired value was achieved early. For a negative cause, value is no longer achievable. The sponsor holds decision authority, and the project manager analyzes, recommends and carries out closure.

2.title: Part 2 Recap
2.text: Let us recap Part 2. Prefer outcome metrics to inputs and leading to lagging indicators, with metrics that are specific and reconciled. Know the pitfalls: the Hawthorne effect, vanity metrics, demoralization, misuse, bias and correlation. Analysis runs from thresholds to cause, forecast, options, change request and report. Report by audience, explain red and amber, and add exception reports. Keep artifacts tailored, current, findable and assessed. In agile work, report accepted increments rather than percent complete. And a project ends in one of five ways, with value as the primary factor. In Part 3, we run the closure sequence.

3.title: The Closure Sequence
3.text: Closure has five gates. One, set the criteria for closing successfully, agreed early and kept current. Two, obtain acceptance: verified deliverables are formally accepted, and vendors' work is accepted. Three, validate readiness for transition: the receiver can operate or continue the work. Four, conclude activities: financials, procurement, resources, records, final lessons and the final report. Five, authorize completion: the sponsor or governance authorizes closure, and stakeholders are informed. If a gate is not passed, fix or renegotiate and check again.

3.title: Determine Closure Criteria
3.text: Define closure criteria early, in the charter, the plan, the contract and the benefits plan, with the sponsor and customer. Make them measurable and agreed. Product and scope: deliverables meet acceptance criteria and are formally accepted. Quality and compliance: verification complete, and operational, safety and regulatory checks passed. Administrative: documents updated, issues resolved, costs charged, accounts closed. Contractual: the seller's work accepted, claims and warranties finalized, invoices paid. Transition: receivers trained, documentation and support ready, risks transferred. Knowledge and value: lessons captured, records archived, a value plan and a benefits owner.

3.title: Three Kinds of Done
3.text: Do not mix three kinds of done. Acceptance criteria apply to each deliverable. The definition of done applies to each backlog item or increment. Closure criteria apply to the project or phase. Suppose every story in the last release met the definition of done, but the contract lists closure criteria such as final documentation and a security sign-off. The project is not finished. Check the closure criteria separately. In adaptive work, when funding ends, agree closure criteria and transfer the remaining backlog to the product owner.

3.title: Obtain Stakeholder Approval of Completion
3.text: The chain is: verify, accept, authorize, inform. Quality control verifies correctness. The customer formally accepts against the acceptance criteria. The sponsor or governance authorizes completion. Then inform all stakeholders. Passing quality control is not acceptance, and silence is not acceptance. Hold a formal acceptance review and document it with a signed acceptance, minutes and a closure notice. If acceptance is refused, record the reasons, fix and re-verify, treat new requests as change requests, and do not close. Engage a new sponsor before closure.

3.title: Validate Readiness for Transition
3.text: Scope complete is not transition ready. Check eight things. People and skills: the receivers have done the work with support, not only watched demonstrations. Documentation and knowledge, including tacit knowledge captured from people who are leaving. The support model. Environment and access, with cut-over tested. Verification and compliance. Open items and risks, accepted or transitioned with owners. Ownership: the receiving owner accepts in writing, and a benefits owner is set. And communication to users. If people holding critical knowledge are leaving soon, capture it from them first.

3.title: Conclude Activities
3.text: Conclude activities in eight areas. Financial: all costs charged, accounts closed. Contractual: every contract closed first. Resources: reassign or release people, address excess materials, release facilities and equipment. Records: collect, audit and archive in a controlled repository. Knowledge: a final lessons session, even if retrospectives ran every iteration, and update process assets. Obligations: verify that contractual, regulatory, legal, social and environmental obligations are met. Risks and issues: resolved or transferred with owners. And the final report.

3.title: Closing Contracts
3.text: Closing a contract has five steps. Accept the external source's work formally. Finalize open claims, guarantees and warranties. Pay all invoices due. Resolve disputes or refer them to the dispute board. And update the records with the final results and archive the information. Every contract must be closed before the project is. Do not close the project with open claims, unpaid invoices or unresolved disputes. A terminated project settles contracts under their termination provisions: accept and pay for what was delivered, and finalize claims.

3.title: The Final Report and Lessons
3.text: The final report summarizes performance. It describes the project or phase, and the evidence that completion criteria were met. It gives quality, cost and schedule results with reasons for variances. It covers validation of the final product, benefits and business needs achieved or expected, and the risks and issues met. Assess success or failure against objectives, the business case and benefits. Hold a final lessons session and update process assets, forwarding suggestions for improving organizational policies to their owners. Measure stakeholder satisfaction, and tell everyone the project is closed. Archive records in a controlled repository.

3.title: Early Termination and Cancelled Projects
3.text: A terminated project still closes formally. PMBOK 8 expects procedures to investigate and document the reasons for early termination and to engage the relevant stakeholders. Document the work delivered, and decide what can be transitioned or reused. Settle contracts under their termination provisions. Release people and resources. Capture lessons and archive records. And communicate the decision and its reasons. For a positive cause, confirm the value with the sponsor, transition what exists and release unused funds. For a negative cause, be transparent about why, and protect people and relationships.

3.title: Benefits After Closure
3.text: Value and benefits outlast the project. The business case and the benefits management plan are business documents, developed before the project and referenced after it ends. The benefits owner monitors, records and reports realized benefits over the planned timeframe. The project manager hands this over with the metrics and does not stay accountable for benefits indefinitely. As exam practice, a post-implementation review some time later checks whether the intended benefits materialized. Oversight may continue after deliverables are finalized but before formal closure, for benefits realization and sustainment.

3.title: Case Check-In: Closing the Microgrid
3.text: Closing our microgrid follows the sequence. Each deliverable is formally accepted against its criteria, and Elena Vasquez authorizes completion. Campus Facilities perform the commissioning tasks with support before handover: watching is not doing. Close the BrightArray, VoltStore and Harlow Construction contracts first, after verifying obligations. Then hand the benefits management plan, baselines and metrics to Campus Operations, the benefits owner. Hold a final lessons session, archive the records, and release the team.

3.title: Closure in Predictive, Agile and Hybrid Work
3.text: Closure looks different by approach. Predictive: closure at phases and the project, with gates, formal acceptance against criteria with sign-off, and exit criteria in the plan and contract. Open items go to owners. Agile: closure at iteration, release and product, with stakeholder review against the definition of done, and closure criteria agreed when funding ends. Unfinished backlog goes to the product owner, because unfinished value belongs to the product, not the project. The project may close while the product continues. Hybrid: formal for the baselined parts, review-based for increments.

3.title: Closure Traps: What PMI Expects
3.text: The traps for closure. Passing tests is not acceptance, and silence is not acceptance. Each phase closes formally with acceptance. Scope complete is not transition ready: finish readiness work before handover. Financial closure and contract closure come first. A terminated project still closes formally, and sunk costs are ignored. The sponsor or governance authorizes completion, not the project manager alone. Value outlasts the project, so name a benefits owner. New requests after acceptance go through change control as new work. Do not close on schedule and budget alone.

3.title: Module Recap
3.text: Let us recap the whole module. Execute: follow the plan, change it through the process, record data and remove blockers. Report: use outcome metrics, honest status for each audience and current artifacts. Accept: deliverables are verified and formally accepted, and the sponsor authorizes completion. Hand over: ready receivers, closed contracts and a benefits owner. Learn: a final lessons session, archived records and updated process assets. Now it is time to test yourself. Five questions follow. For each one, pause the video, choose your answer, and then listen to the explanation.

3.title: Practice Question 1
3.text: Question one. A vendor delivers a pump with a higher capacity than specified, at no extra cost, and the team wants to install it because it passed its tests. What should the project manager do? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is B. Even free upgrades need impact assessment, and passing tests does not replace configuration review, so the change goes through change control. Installing it, rejecting it automatically, or updating records afterward all skip the assessment.

3.title: Practice Question 2
3.text: Question two. Two teams keep missing handoffs, and the project manager is considering adding a weekly review meeting. What is the best action? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is D. Missed handoffs are fixed at the source by defining the handoff, who is responsible and how completion is confirmed, rather than adding meetings. More meetings, informal coordination, or more reports leave the handoff itself undefined.

3.title: Practice Question 3
3.text: Question three. A team meets its velocity target every sprint, but surveys show that clients rarely use the new features. What should the project manager do? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is A. Velocity is output, not value, so the project manager adds usage and outcome measures to show whether the features create value. Raising the target, dropping the measure, or declaring success ignores the outcome gap.

3.title: Practice Question 4
3.text: Question four. All tests on the final deliverable passed, and the vendor says the work is complete. The customer has not responded to the acceptance request. What should the project manager do? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is C. Passing quality control is verification, not acceptance, and silence is not acceptance, so a formal review with the customer is needed. Treating silence as acceptance, marking it accepted, or repeating tests skip the customer's formal acceptance.

3.title: Practice Question 5
3.text: Question five. A new system is complete and accepted, but the operations staff who will run it have only watched demonstrations. The project is scheduled to close next week. What should the project manager do? The four options are on the screen. Choose your answer. The answer is B. Scope complete is not transition ready, so the receivers must perform the work with support before the formal handover and closure. Leaving training to operations, handing over manuals, or an open-ended extension do not confirm readiness.

3.title: Answers at a Glance
3.text: Here are all five answers together. Question one: B. Even a free upgrade needs impact assessment and change control. Question two: D. Define handoffs and confirmation points instead of adding meetings. Question three: A. Velocity is output, so add usage and outcome measures. Question four: C. Verified is not accepted, and silence is not acceptance. Question five: B. Scope complete is not transition ready, so finish hands-on training first. That completes Module 9. Next, Module 10 covers project governance and compliance. See you there.
